heritage.name: Teochew Chinese
heritage.homeland: Chaoshan, eastern Guangdong — Chaozhou, Shantou and Jieyang
heritage.migrationStory: Teochew migrants travelled especially to Thailand, Singapore, Malaya, Cambodia and Vietnam during the 18th–20th centuries. Many built livelihoods in farming, rice trading, retail and other businesses.
heritage.funFact: Teochew and Hokkien are both Southern Min language varieties, but their speech is distinctly different.

research.culture: Chinese, especially Hokkien and Teochew; also Korean
research.meaning: 林 means “woods” or “grove.” The character combines two 木 characters, each meaning “tree.”
research.summary: Lim is most often a Southern Min spelling of the Chinese surname 林, written Lín in Mandarin. It is especially associated with Hokkien and Teochew families in Southeast Asia, though Lim is also a well-established Korean spelling of the same character.
research.originStory: A traditional Chinese account traces 林 to the family of Bi Gan, a royal adviser executed by the last Shang king. His pregnant wife reportedly escaped into the woods, where their son Jian was born; King Wu of Zhou later granted him the surname Lin in recognition of that refuge. This is a cherished ancestral tradition, not a genealogy that can be independently verified for every Lim family.

timeline.event: The surname’s best-known origin legend connects Bi Gan’s son with the founding of the Zhou dynasty.
Successive migrations carried northern Chinese families, including Lin lineages, into Fujian.
Lin lineages became deeply established in Fujian and eastern Guangdong, the homelands of many Hokkien and Teochew Lims.
Families from southeastern China settled in Taiwan and maritime Southeast Asia through trade and migration.
Large Hokkien and Teochew migrations helped establish Lim as a familiar surname in Singapore, Malaya, Indonesia and the Philippines.

heritageOptions.name: Hokkien Chinese
heritageOptions.homeland: Southern Fujian — Quanzhou, Zhangzhou and Xiamen
heritageOptions.migrationStory: Hokkien families crossed to Taiwan and settled throughout Southeast Asian trading ports over several centuries. Migration expanded in the 19th and early 20th centuries through commerce, labour recruitment and family networks.
heritageOptions.funFact: Hokkien speakers helped make Lim a familiar surname in ports from Singapore to Manila.

heritageOptions.name: Teochew Chinese
heritageOptions.homeland: Chaoshan, eastern Guangdong — Chaozhou, Shantou and Jieyang
heritageOptions.migrationStory: Teochew migrants travelled especially to Thailand, Singapore, Malaya, Cambodia and Vietnam during the 18th–20th centuries. Many built livelihoods in farming, rice trading, retail and other businesses.
heritageOptions.funFact: Teochew and Hokkien are both Southern Min language varieties, but their speech is distinctly different.

heritageOptions.name: Korean Im/Lim clans
heritageOptions.homeland: Korea — several ancestral clan seats, including Naju and Pyeongtaek
heritageOptions.migrationStory: Korean families migrated to China’s northeast, the Russian Far East and Hawaii from the late 19th century onward. Later migrations carried Lim families to North America and other destinations.
heritageOptions.funFact: Korean families distinguish surname lineages by bon-gwan, an ancestral clan seat, rather than surname alone.

famousBearers.name: Lim Bo Seng
famousBearers.note: Singapore-based resistance organiser who died in Japanese captivity in 1944.

famousBearers.name: Lim Goh Tong
famousBearers.note: Fujian-born Malaysian entrepreneur who founded the Genting Group.

famousBearers.name: Lim Swee Say
famousBearers.note: Singaporean former cabinet minister and labour movement leader.

funFacts: Lim, Lin, Lam and Lâm can all represent the same Chinese character, 林.
The surname’s character looks like its meaning: two trees standing together.
林 appears in the traditional Chinese Hundred Family Surnames text.
Chinese clan associations often link Lim families through ancestral villages and shared migration histories.
In Korea, Lim is a common family spelling even though standard South Korean romanization gives Im.
research.caveat: Lim strongly suggests Hokkien or Teochew ancestry in a Southeast Asian context, but it does not prove either. Korean Lim usually represents 林, though some 임 families use 任, a different surname character. An ancestral village, original written surname or Korean clan seat is much more informative than the English spelling alone.

outline.title: The Grove Across the Sea
outline.tagline: Two wooden trees, two distant homes, and one girl searching for the missing half.
outline.logline: When thirteen-year-old Wei Ling Lim discovers half a wooden grove in her Singapore home, she is swept into a Teochew family's journey from Chaoshan to Singapore. Following this fictional ancestral thread through migration, plantation work and wartime survival, she must find the matching half to return home.

heirloom.name: The Two-Tree Token
heirloom.description: A palm-sized wooden plaque carved with 林, split between its two 木 characters so that each half carries one tree. Wei Ling finds one half inside an old wooden document box; touching it while reading the family's letters draws her into the moments they describe, but only joining both halves will bring her home.

outline.mystery: Where is the other half of the wooden grove?

cast.name: A-Sheng Lim
cast.role: Wei Ling's fictional ancestor and first companion in the past
cast.look: Seventeen in 1869, lean, with bright eyes, a small notch in his left eyebrow and black hair worn in a Qing-era queue; indigo cotton jacket and patched trousers. In later acts, retain the eyebrow notch while adding grey hair and a stooped posture.

cast.name: Mei
cast.role: A-Sheng's mother, who remains in Chaoshan
cast.look: Forty-two in 1869, compact build, broad cheekbones and centre-parted hair in a low bun; dark cotton tunic, practical trousers and a faded blue cloth tucked into her waistband.

cast.name: Ah Lan Lim
cast.role: A-Sheng's Singapore-born granddaughter and keeper of the family box
cast.look: Ten in 1905, round-faced, with a mole beneath her right eye and two short braids; pale cotton blouse and dark trousers. As an adult, keep the mole, replace the braids with a low bun, and give her a brown document satchel.

cast.name: Mr Tan
cast.role: Plantation overseer and early source of conflict
cast.look: About forty in 1870, wiry, narrow-faced, with a thin moustache; rolled-sleeve white cotton shirt, dark trousers and a ledger always tucked beneath one arm.

acts.title: One Tree in a Box
acts.beat: Wei Ling, thirteen, with a long ponytail and bright curious eyes, discovers a wooden document box containing old letters and half a token whose carving resembles 木. When she traces the incomplete 林 beside a letter mentioning Chaoshan, the room becomes a village courtyard, and she learns that finding the other tree is her only way home.
acts.history: 林 means woods or grove, and Lim is a Teochew rendering of the same surname character also represented by spellings such as Lin and Lam.

acts.title: The Tree That Stays
acts.place: A fictional village near Jieyang, Chaoshan, eastern Guangdong
acts.beat: Wei Ling befriends A-Sheng as his household struggles with poor harvests, debts and too little work, while a relative's letter offers an introduction to employment in Singapore. Mei divides a locally carved 林 token between herself and her departing son; Wei Ling watches her place the other half inside a blue cloth pouch, but the heirloom pulls Wei Ling onward before she can reach it.
acts.history: Nineteenth-century Teochew migration grew through household pressures and overseas kinship networks; Mei also tells the Bi Gan surname legend, explicitly identifying it as ancestral tradition rather than a verified genealogy.

acts.title: Beyond the Harbour
acts.place: Shantou, Hong Kong and the South China Sea
acts.beat: A-Sheng and Wei Ling travel through Shantou and Hong Kong toward Singapore, carrying bedding, an introduction letter and his half of the token. Rough weather soaks their baggage, and Wei Ling helps save the letter that may secure his first job, discovering that the voyage's real lifeline is another person's promise.
acts.history: Shantou opened as a treaty port in 1860, and its expanding shipping connections helped carry Chaoshan migrants into maritime Southeast Asia.

acts.title: The Bitter Leaf
acts.place: A gambier and pepper plantation in the Seletar area, Singapore
acts.beat: A-Sheng finds work cutting gambier leaves and tending pepper, but Mr Tan's account book makes his passage advance and purchases difficult to repay. Wei Ling helps him compare the entries with his remembered wages, and support from fellow workers forces a correction, allowing him to send his first money and letter home.
acts.history: Teochew workers and entrepreneurs played major roles in nineteenth-century Singapore's gambier-and-pepper economy, whose plantations extended across the island's interior.

acts.title: Letters Build a Bridge
acts.place: A small rice shop near Boat Quay, Singapore
acts.beat: Now an older shopkeeper, A-Sheng introduces Wei Ling to his granddaughter Ah Lan, who helps sort correspondence while learning to weigh rice and keep accounts. A parcel sent after Mei's death finally brings her half of the token to Singapore, but before Wei Ling can join the pieces, the box pulls her into a later letter marked by wartime fear.
acts.history: Qiaopi—overseas Chinese letters commonly accompanied by remittances—connected migrant households with relatives in China, while Singapore's riverfront trade supported livelihoods such as rice dealing and retail.

acts.title: What the Box Protected
acts.beat: During the Japanese occupation, adult Ah Lan shelters the family papers and Mei's token half beneath the box's loose bottom board, while Wei Ling witnesses shortages, fear and the devastating loss of neighbours during Sook Ching. The next letter carries her to 1965, when an elderly Ah Lan repairs the box for her descendants and tells Wei Ling to look beneath what everyone thought was its floor.
acts.history: Singapore endured Japanese occupation from 1942 to 1945, including the Sook Ching massacre, before achieving internal self-government in 1959 and becoming independent on 9 August 1965.

acts.title: Two Trees, One Grove
acts.beat: Wei Ling lifts the hidden board, finds Mei's half and joins the two trees, returning to her own room with the complete 林 in her hands. She shares the letters with her family and begins recording their actual memories, understanding that the surname legend is inherited tradition, while her own family's history must be pieced together from evidence and voices.
acts.history: Family letters, remittance records, oral histories and clan-association records can help investigate particular migration stories, but a shared surname alone does not establish a documented ancestral line.

pages.place: Singapore and a village near Jieyang, Chaoshan
pages.recap: Wei Ling Lim is thirteen and lives in Singapore. She wants to learn why her family has kept an old box of letters.
pages.heroOutfit: A yellow short-sleeved T-shirt, navy blue knee-length shorts, white ankle socks and red canvas trainers. Her long hair stays in a ponytail throughout.

panels.setting: Wei Ling's family home, Singapore, present day
panels.scene: The hero is alone in her family's living room, sorting a shelf of family keepsakes. An old wooden document box sits beside a family photograph.
panels.caption: Singapore, today. Wei Ling Lim, thirteen, is sorting family keepsakes alone.

dialogue.speaker: Wei Ling
dialogue.text: What story are you hiding?

panels.setting: Wei Ling's family home, Singapore, present day
panels.scene: The hero lifts the box from the shelf with both hands. Its lid bears the surname character 林, and a folded modern family note is tucked beneath its cord.

dialogue.speaker: Wei Ling
dialogue.text: That's our surname on the lid!

panels.setting: Wei Ling's family home, Singapore, present day
panels.scene: The hero unfolds the family note. Beneath its short message is a simple drawing showing 林 as two trees.
panels.caption: The family note explains why the box was kept.

dialogue.speaker: Wei Ling
dialogue.text: Keep these letters. They tell our family's story.

panels.setting: Wei Ling's family home, Singapore, present day
panels.scene: The hero opens the box on the table. Inside are old letters, modern English translations and half a palm-sized wooden plaque, carved with one 木; its broken edge is clearly visible.
panels.caption: Inside: family letters, their translations, and half a wooden token.

dialogue.speaker: Wei Ling
dialogue.text: One tree? Where's the other?

Soft daylight enters from an unseen window at left; warm wood, cream walls, and gentle natural colours keep the room consistent. No other people are present.

characters.name: Wei Ling
characters.action: Same ponytail and outfit as in every panel; she peers into the open box with raised eyebrows and puzzled curiosity, one hand near the contents without obscuring them.

panels.setting: Wei Ling's family home, Singapore, present day
panels.scene: The hero compares the token with the note's drawing. She places its single tree beneath one half of 林, showing exactly where the missing piece belongs.
panels.caption: Two trees make 林: woods or grove. One tree is missing.

dialogue.speaker: Wei Ling
dialogue.text: Two trees make Lim. This is only half.

panels.setting: Wei Ling's family home, Singapore, present day
panels.scene: The hero selects a translated letter beside its fragile original. The translation identifies a village near Jieyang in Chaoshan, China, and the year 1869.
panels.caption: One letter points to Chaoshan, her family's homeland in China.

dialogue.speaker: Wei Ling
dialogue.text: Jieyang. 1869. Who wrote this?

panels.setting: Wei Ling's family home, Singapore, present day
panels.scene: While reading the translation, the hero traces the wooden tree with her thumb. Light spills from the broken edge, and glowing words appear above the letter.
panels.caption: Join both trees to go home.

dialogue.speaker: Wei Ling
dialogue.text: Home? I'm already home!

panels.setting: Wei Ling's family home, Singapore, present day
panels.scene: Still gripping the token, the hero reaches for the table as the room dissolves around her. Wooden shelves fade into courtyard walls, and the tiled floor becomes packed earth.
panels.caption: The token pulls Wei Ling into the letter's past.

dialogue.speaker: Wei Ling
dialogue.text: Wait! I haven't found the other tree!

art.locations: Wei Ling's family living room in Singapore, present day: a warm, tidy room with pale cream walls, dark wooden shelves, and a sturdy wooden table. characters.name: Wei Ling
characters.position: right foreground, face turned toward the letter
characters.action: In the same outfit, she traces the carved tree with her thumb. Her eyes widen in startled disbelief as the token glows.

panels.composition: Wide, dynamic shot at table height. The room visibly dissolves from left to right: wooden shelves fade into courtyard walls and tiled flooring breaks into packed earth. characters.name: Wei Ling
characters.action: Still gripping the broken wooden token, she reaches toward the table to steady herself, body twisting as the room transforms around her. Her expression is alarmed, mouth open, ponytail swinging; her yellow T-shirt, navy shorts, white ankle socks and red trainers remain unchanged.

panels.setting: Village courtyard near Jieyang, Chaoshan, China, 1869
panels.scene: The hero lands on her knees in a village courtyard, still holding the token. Low houses surround her; her living room and the box are gone.
panels.caption: A village near Jieyang, Chaoshan, China. 1869.

dialogue.speaker: Wei Ling
dialogue.text: That was not a normal family keepsake.

panels.setting: Village courtyard near Jieyang, Chaoshan, China, 1869
panels.scene: A-Sheng Lim steps out of a doorway and offers the hero his hand. He has a notch in his left eyebrow, a long queue, an indigo cotton jacket and patched trousers.
panels.caption: A-Sheng Lim, seventeen: Wei Ling's ancestor, though she doesn't know it yet.

dialogue.speaker: A-Sheng Lim
dialogue.text: Are you hurt?

dialogue.speaker: Wei Ling
dialogue.text: Only my idea of a normal afternoon.

panels.setting: Village courtyard near Jieyang, Chaoshan, China, 1869
panels.scene: Back on her feet, the hero shows A-Sheng the broken token. He leans closer to examine its carved tree.

dialogue.speaker: Wei Ling
dialogue.text: I need its other half to get home.

dialogue.speaker: A-Sheng Lim
dialogue.text: My mother knows that carving.

panels.setting: Village courtyard near Jieyang, Chaoshan, China, 1869
panels.scene: A-Sheng points toward the dark doorway. The hero takes one step toward it, but her token suddenly tugs sideways in her hand, pulling toward a narrow courtyard gate instead.
panels.caption: One clue leads inside. The token pulls another way.

dialogue.speaker: A-Sheng Lim
dialogue.text: Come. We'll ask her.

dialogue.speaker: Wei Ling
dialogue.text: Then why is it pulling toward the gate?

Overcast daylight is soft and muted, with cool grey masonry, earthy browns, and restrained indigo accents. No modern objects or traces of Wei Ling’s vanished living room or box.

historyNote.title: Did you know? Two trees make a grove
historyNote.body: The Chinese character 林 means woods or grove and combines two 木 characters, each meaning tree. Lim is a Teochew spelling of 林; Lin and Lam can represent the same surname character in other language traditions. A shared surname alone does not prove that two families share a documented ancestor.

quiz.question: What does the surname character 林 mean?
quiz.explanation: 林 combines two tree characters and means woods or grove.

pages.place: A village near Jieyang, Chaoshan, China
pages.recap: Wei Ling needs the missing half of a wooden token to return home. She follows its pull through the gate, with A-Sheng close behind.
pages.heroOutfit: A yellow short-sleeved T-shirt, navy blue knee-length shorts, white ankle socks and red canvas trainers. Her long hair stays in a ponytail throughout.

Keep architecture, props, weather and light consistent whenever these connected yards appear; avoid modern objects.

art.locations: Neighbouring work yard near Jieyang, Chaoshan, China, 1869: a compact, packed-earth courtyard beside a modest traditional home with pale, weathered plaster walls, dark timber framing, and a simple tiled roof visible above. A narrow lane opens beyond the yard. A low work surface, the bedding bundle, and a grain basket remain unobtrusive continuity props. Soft overcast daylight gives the scene muted earth browns, grey plaster, and natural indigo and faded-blue accents. The air is still; in the final panel only, the lane and far edge of the yard distort into a faint, distant harbour as a supernatural transition, while the courtyard itself remains recognizable.

historyNote.title: Did you know? A letter could open a door
historyNote.body: In the nineteenth century, many Teochew people left Chaoshan for work in Southeast Asia. Poor harvests, debts and limited work could influence a household's decision to send someone abroad. Relatives and people from the same home village often helped newcomers find lodging or employment. A-Sheng and Mei are fictional, but their letter shows how these real connections could help migrants.

It guaranteed that he would become rich.
quiz.explanation: His relative offered an introduction that could help him find work, not guaranteed wealth.
